title: Ring of Neighbor Sums
statement:
The array code is arranged in a ring: after the last element comes the first one again, and before the first comes the last. You also get an integer k.

Build a new array of the same length where position i holds:

  • if k > 0: the sum of the k elements right after i around the ring,
  • if k < 0: the sum of the |k| elements right before i,
  • if k = 0: 0.

Element i itself is never part of its own sum. All positions use the original values, not the ones you have already replaced.

examples.why: Position 2 takes 5 and then wraps around to 2: 5 + 2 = 7. Position 3 wraps right away: 2 + 7 = 9.
Each position takes the element just before it; position 0 wraps around to the last one, 5.
With k = 0 every sum is empty.

hints: Summing k elements for every position is O(n · k). Neighboring positions share almost all of their elements.
Moving from position i to i + 1, the window loses one element on its left end and gains one on its right end.
For k > 0 the window for 0 is indexes 1..k; for k < 0 it is n − |k| .. n − 1. Slide it with indexes taken modulo n.

explain.intuition:
Every position's sum covers a block of |k| consecutive ring positions, and the block for i + 1 is the block for i shifted by one. So compute the first block once, then for each step subtract the element that leaves and add the element that enters. Taking indexes modulo n handles the wrap.

The two directions differ only in where the first block sits: for k > 0 it is 1..k, for k < 0 it is the last |k| positions n − |k| .. n − 1. After that the slide is identical, which keeps the code to one loop.
steps: If k === 0, return an array of zeros.
Set the window [start, end]: [1, k] if k > 0, else [n + k, n − 1].
For each i: store the sum, then subtract code[start % n], add code[(end + 1) % n], and move both ends by one.
pitfalls: Writing results into code while you still read from it. Later sums need the original values.
Getting the negative window wrong by one, for example including position i itself.
Using % on a negative index in JavaScript. -1 % 4 is -1, not 3; add n first.

solutions.title: Sum each window from scratch
solutions.idea: For every position, walk |k| steps in the right direction and add them up.

solutions.title: Sliding window around the ring
solutions.idea: Sum the first window once; each step drops one element and adds the next one, with indexes modulo n.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def ringSums(self, code: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        n = len(code)
        out = [0] * n
        if k == 0:
            return out
        start, end = (1, k) if k > 0 else (n + k, n - 1)
        total = sum(code[i % n] for i in range(start, end + 1))
        for i in range(n):
            out[i] = total
            total -= code[start % n]
            start += 1
            end += 1
            total += code[end % n]
        return out
